vignette:
He tells the story quietly, his voice flat but his hands never still-fidgeting with the edge of his sleeve, a loose thread on his jeans. He is a plumber, fifty years old, married for twenty-two years to a woman he met when they both worked in a hospital kitchen in Dar es Salaam. They have three grown children, all living abroad now. He came to the United States fifteen years ago, built a life, learned the trade, bought a van with his own tools racked neatly in the back. That van is where the story begins.

It happened on a Tuesday afternoon in November. He had been called to a townhouse near the university to repair a leaking toilet in the basement. The customer-a man in his late twenties, he guesses-let him in, showed him the bathroom, then closed the door behind him. He was on his knees, wrench in hand, when he heard the lock click. He thought nothing of it at first. Then he heard voices, two or three people, and footsteps. The door swung open. The customer was there with two others. They accused him of stealing-"You people always steal"-though he had not touched anything. Before he could explain, the customer swung a metal pipe, the same kind he carries in his truck for plumbing work. He remembers the sound of it hitting his skull, the wet crack that seemed to come from somewhere else. Then the kicks, the shouting, the taste of blood and floor grime. They left him on the basement floor, unconscious.

He woke in the hospital with a concussion, three broken ribs, and a shattered sense of safety. The police never found the men. He filed a report, but nothing came of it. He went back to work after six weeks, because the bills would not pause. But something had shifted. He cannot be in a basement now. Any basement. The smell of damp concrete makes his stomach clench. He avoids houses with narrow stairwells, making excuses to his dispatcher-"Too far, too small, send someone else." He has lost three jobs this month alone. The other night he drove forty minutes to a job, saw the basement entrance, and turned around. He told the customer he forgot his tools. He knows they are starting to talk.

At home, he has become a man his wife barely recognizes. He startles at the sound of a door closing. He checks the locks three times before bed. He sleeps in the living room now, on the couch, facing the front door, a claw hammer under the cushion. She asks him why, and he says, "Just in case," but he cannot explain what he means. He does not go to the grocery store alone. He avoids crowds, loud voices, anyone who looks at him too long. The other day a young man in a hoodie walked toward him on the sidewalk-just a college student, probably-and he crossed the street, heart pounding, sweat breaking on his forehead. He felt ashamed, then angry at himself, then ashamed again.

He replays the assault every night. Not the whole thing-just the moment before the pipe came down. The customer's face. The way he said "you people." He wonders if his dark skin and his accent made him a target. He wonders if the men are still out there. He wonders if he will ever walk into a stranger's house again without his hands shaking. He told me, "I used to fix things. That was all I was. Now I am broken, and I don't know what to fix first." He is tired. He is holding on, but barely.
